I'm not in any way saying this films reputation isn't deserved and I can understand why so many people like it, but it just didn't work for me, sadly, because I had high expectations.

Much like "2001: A Space Odyssey", "Alien" is a film in which I can tell a lot of passion, talent & work went into it, & I can definitely see why so many love it & praise it as a masterpiece, I just personally couldn't really get into it & it's not really for me. The film is very well made with great direction, cinematography, acting & some extremely impressive effects that still hold up well today. However it's also a sci-fi & space film. Two film genres I don't like, & this leads to me finding the film pretty dull in regards to the setting & concepts on display. Doesn't help that most of the characters & dialogue are similarly boring & uninteresting (Besides Ripley & Parker, who I actually found to be pretty interesting characters due to some pretty great performances & actually having defined, interesting personalities & dialogue). However I will say I did actually quite like the last 40 or so minutes which I found really gripping & intense for the most part. Weaver's performance combined with the great tension & special effects really worked together to make some pretty gripping scenes in a way I didn't really feel the film did before. Overall, it's well made no doubt & I definitely see why so many love it. But  it just isn't really for me, on the whole I find it to be pretty dull & uninteresting. Even if it does have some enjoyable elements near the end. Still, not enough to keep it from feeling like a below average viewing experience. Well made, I just didn't like it.

Upon landing, a crew member is attacked by a parasitic organism, bringing an agile, ruthless extraterrestrial creature aboard their vessel. Trapped inside the claustrophobic metallic corridors of their ship, the crew is hunted one by one as they fight for survival. Blending brilliant production design, dread-inducing tension, and groundbreaking practical effects, the film established a timeless blueprint for cinematic horror. Plutôt actuel quand on prend en considération le fait que leur mère est un ordinateur et qu’ils vivent en son sein. Ils sont les cobayes d’une évolution qui les dépasse. Des pions qui consentent inconsciemment à obéir à une intelligence froide qui elle même répond à des ordres froidement conçus, afin de répondre à des intérêts de personnes extérieures. Les robots sont les alliés de certains humains au détriment d’autres. Ash et Ripley sont souvent en conflit. Intéressant de voir comment on considérait la forme de vie extra-terrestre (au sens littéral) : l’alien est un parasite qui tue et utilise le corps humain. C’est un danger et quelque chose qui ne nous intéresse que dans le cadre de la science et de sa dissection. L’alien est un organisme comme l’être humain mais sans conscience : pur pour le robot, monstrueux pour nous. C’est un rappel de la valeur de notre nature. Ripley est la voix de la raison et de la mesure, elle est calme et réfléchie depuis le début, protège la communauté quand les hommes ne font que ce qui est dans leur intérêt personnel. Merci de souligner ça. Ce qui est valable dans l'espace est aussi valable sur Terre. Elle se retrouve aux prises avec la loi : elle la suit pour le bien commun avant de se rendre compte qu’elle est injuste. L'esthétique est sombre et nous donne l’impression de ne rien contrôler. Nous vivons ce voyage au même titre que les véritables passagers, ce qui est renforcé par les mouvements de caméra : nous sommes avec eux, vivons les mêmes choses, car la caméra nous feinte. Nous ne pouvons nous croire omniscients, extérieurs, car même quand nous avons l'impression qu'elle nous guide pour nous montrer quelque chose que les personnages ne voient pas, il se passe souvent rien. Enfermée dans son scaphandre, il semble la protéger. Pourtant, elle n’a jamais été aussi  vulnérable. L'être humain est bien vulnérable.

Alien is obviously a legendary film, and I did like it overall, but I constantly had this weird feeling that I liked the film more in theory than I actually did in practice. Because when I describe Alien, it sounds amazing. A working crew in space picks up a strange signal, lands on this planet and discovers this completely alien biomechanical environment filled with eggs. Then you have the entire plot with Ash, the company secretly wanting the organism and basically considering the crew expendable. You have the whole development of the alien itself. And, most importantly, you have the cat. I genuinely think I cared more about that cat surviving than anyone else. Absolute main character. If the cat had died, I would have left this film genuinely angry. And then there is the Xenomorph. Now THAT is what I call an alien. The design is basically perfect. It looks unbelievably tough. I also love that they actually built a full suit and had someone physically perform as the creature. Some moments definitely show the limitations of that, but I still really appreciate the practical approach. Everything based on H. R. Giger's artwork is incredible. I absolutely love this biomechanical, cosmic, almost mythical aesthetic. Every time the film gave me more of it, I wanted even more. The alien environment and especially the place with all the eggs might honestly be the visual highlight of the entire film for me. The lighting is also beautiful. All those lights shining through smoke, the helmets, the interiors of the ship, the way everything is illuminated. There is so much visually that I really like here. Probably my favorite decision in the entire film is how long it takes before we actually see the fully grown Xenomorph. Instead, we basically watch its entire development. First there is the egg and the little guy that hugs your face, then the thing bursts out of Kane's chest and runs away ridiculously fast, which I somehow found kind of cute, and eventually this tiny creature becomes this gigantic monster in an absurdly short amount of time. I love that progression. You know what the final creature looks like, but the film makes you wait for it. You first see all these different stages before eventually getting the full-grown Xenomorph. I think that was an extremely good decision. I also genuinely did not see the Ash reveal coming. For quite a while I thought Ripley was basically the only competent person on the entire ship, although I started reconsidering that during the second half. My main problem is simply that all of this worked better for me as a concept than as an actual viewing experience. When I describe all these individual elements, Alien sounds incredible. The company, Ash, the Xenomorph, its life cycle, Giger's designs, the crew trapped in space. There are so many cool ingredients here. But if I separate the film from its historical importance and reputation and only ask myself what I actually got pound for pound on the screen, I just wasn't that engaged by it. I wouldn't call it boring, but parts of it definitely dragged for me. And especially once the Xenomorph is fully established, the concept becomes relatively straightforward. The alien is somewhere on the ship, the crew tries to survive, and it starts killing them. There wasn't really another mystery for me to crack or another idea that kept developing. At some point I basically understood the situation and then watched it play out. For a horror film, I also never really got that nerve-racking feeling where I'm constantly uncomfortable about what might happen next. The company considering the crew expendable was probably the most interesting idea for me, but the film doesn't really develop that very far either. It's there, and I like it, but it remains more of an element within the larger survival story than something the film seriously explores. So yeah, Alien is a good film. It has an absolutely iconic creature, some incredible designs, great lighting, a really cool reveal with Ash and one of the best cats in cinema. Historically, I completely understand why it's such a huge film. Personally, though, I just wish the experience of actually watching it had been as exciting to me as the film sounds when I talk about it.

87/100 A pioneer of deep-space horror. The film's mastery of suspense and atmosphere lies in its refusal to fully reveal the creature, keeping it at the edge of our visual perception. Partial glimpses, spatial concealment and sound cues sustain a fear rooted in the unknown. The Nostromo becomes a floating industrial prison, its metallic corridors, dim lighting, narrow passages and constant mechanical hum forming an oppressive, claustrophobic environment. Scott's command of spatial depth, lighting and visual concealment gives this sense of confinement its enduring cinematic force. H.R. Giger's biomechanical aesthetic is undoubtedly the film's greatest achievement. Blurring the boundaries between organism and industrial construct, flesh and machinery, it transforms organic life into something deeply alien, imbued with both reproductive imagery and mechanical textures. The creature's skeletal exoskeleton, tubular organs and overtly reproductive forms constitute a distinctive visual language of bodily anxiety. Giger not only gives the film its unmistakable visual identity, but fundamentally reshapes how science-fiction horror imagines the unknown.

I did find the exterior design of the ship a bit too toy-like in its movements, especially compared to *2001: A Space Odyssey*, but it didn't take away from how impressive it was. I liked the idea that our crew are just blue-collar people doing their jobs and waiting to get paid. It reminds me of the type of sci-fi like *The Fifth Element* and *Cowboy Bebop*, where spaceships are as casual as normal commutes, with everyday items incorporated into the futuristic setting. The alien design is iconic, and I was obviously familiar with it before watching the movie. I'm not sure if I'm desensitized to this genre, but it didn't feel like horror until the last few sequences, and only in specific parts. I appreciated the twist in the middle and the well-made ending. Classic for a reason.

This film is extremely similar to John Carpenter’s “The Thing”, just with the addition of the sci-fi element, so it’s to no surprise that I loved it so much. Alien is a masterclass in many fields. Ridley Scott was excellent at crafting this film’s plot, structure, characters, cinematography, and more. It takes its time and provides ideal attention to each. I want to begin with the pacing. I love that this film takes its time all the way through the story. With premise like this, it could’ve easily been a forgettable slasher with a weak story, but instead, it’s so much more than a group trying to survive from a monster. The setting, characters, and plot are well established, creating the perfect atmosphere. We spend lots of time on each, exploring each and creating attachments. Additionally with this plot, the level of fear, suspension, and dread work SO well. It’s a slow burn with incredible payoff, and that’s why this plot and antagonist work so well. It was all built up and created with a purpose, not being wasted at all. The threat of the single Xenemorph is used to its full potential. It gradually builds up to this ultimate threat, and it’s terrifying. I love the decision of how it was used; it wasn’t overdone at all. Instead of being a mass slasher, it was kept hidden, and only used at the perfect moments to pick off the cast. This is what makes the “alien” a classic antagonist, as it carries so much weight without being oversaturated. Speaking of the cast that it picks off, each individual that made it up is the core of this movie. The characters are simply great. Such a well rounded group of protagonists, all acted brilliantly. They have great dynamics that make for a believable story. Sigourney Weaver nails it as Ripley. A very strong main character to root for.
